practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a sector of the media industry?
A) Audio-visual
B) Publishing
C) Animation
D) Photography
practice_questions.marks: B) Publishing [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two types of media product that can be found in the advertising and marketing sector.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct answers, for example: TV commercial / audio-visual [1]; website or landing page / interactive [1]; social media graphic or poster / publishing and print [1]; podcast advertisement / audio [1]. Answers must identify a product type, not just repeat the sector name. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why media products in the contemporary industry often combine more than one media type.
practice_questions.marks: A basic point scores 1 mark (e.g. 'to reach a wider audience'). Development scores 2 marks (e.g. 'because audiences consume content across multiple platforms — TV, social media and websites — a campaign that only uses one product type will miss large groups of its target audience'). A further developed answer with a specific example scores 3 marks (e.g. add 'a film studio releasing a new blockbuster will combine a theatrical trailer (audio-visual), a dedicated website (interactive) and social media image posts (publishing and print) so that audiences encounter the product wherever they spend their time'). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between the television and film sector and the web and app sector. Give one example of a product from each sector.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): television and film produces long-form or short-form moving-image content distributed to passive audiences via broadcast or streaming; the web and app sector creates interactive digital products that users actively navigate, often updated continuously post-launch (2 marks for a clear contrast addressing both sectors; 1 mark for describing only one sector).
Examples (1 mark each): television and film — e.g. a drama series on BBC iPlayer; web and app — e.g. a recipe website or a budgeting mobile app (1 mark each for a correct, sector-appropriate example). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A media company is planning to launch a campaign for a new sports drink targeting young adults aged 16 to 24. The campaign will include products across three different media types.

Discuss the factors the company should consider when deciding which media types and sectors to use for this campaign.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A balanced discussion addressing at least two relevant factors from different angles, applied to the scenario. For example: the need to reach young adults on the platforms they use most (interactive/social media and audio-visual/short-form video) versus the cost and skill requirements of producing high-quality content across multiple media types; or the benefit of combining product types (e.g. audio-visual TV advert + interactive social media campaign + audio podcast sponsorship) to maximise reach, weighed against the risk of spreading the budget too thinly. Both factors developed with reasoning and scenario reference.
Secure (3-4 marks): Two relevant factors identified and briefly explained with some reference to the target audience or campaign context.
Developing (2 marks): One factor identified with limited explanation.
Emerging (1 mark): A vague point about the campaign with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
The media industry has changed significantly over the last two decades, with streaming platforms replacing traditional broadcast TV for many audiences and digital products overtaking print.

Evaluate the extent to which media creators must understand how different sectors and product types work together in order to succeed in today's media industry.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced evaluation that argues understanding cross-sector, multi-product working is essential because modern audiences consume fragmented content across platforms (streaming, social media, apps, podcasts) so single-sector expertise is insufficient; then challenges this with the counter-argument that deep specialisation within one sector remains valuable — a film editor does not need to build apps — and that large productions rely on specialists, not generalists. A clear, substantiated judgement is reached about the relative importance of cross-sector knowledge versus deep specialism, going beyond listing points.
Secure (5-6 marks): At least two relevant points on each side, with some application to the changing media landscape and an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points identified but largely one-sided or without a judgement. Some reference to sectors or product types.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic, undeveloped points about the media industry. [8 marks]

before.exam_tip_html: When asked to identify a media sector or product type, use the correct terminology and back it up with a real or realistic example. Examiners reward specific, applied knowledge — writing "the games sector produces interactive software such as console games and mobile apps" scores more than simply writing "games". If the question asks you to explain how media products combine types, name both product types involved and describe exactly how they work together in a single product or campaign.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a responsibility of the producer on a media production?
A) Making creative decisions about visual style
B) Writing the script and dialogue
C) Managing the budget and schedule
D) Editing the footage in post-production
practice_questions.marks: C) Managing the budget and schedule [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two tasks that take place during the pre-production phase of a media project.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct correct answers, for example: writing a script [1]; creating a storyboard [1]; creating a mood board [1]; planning a schedule or timeline [1]; setting a budget [1]; scouting or selecting locations [1]; sourcing assets (images, music, fonts) [1]. Answers that merely describe production tasks (e.g. filming) score zero. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which the role of a graphic designer differs from the role of an animator.
practice_questions.marks: A basic point scores 1 mark (e.g. 'a graphic designer creates still images'). Development scores 2 marks (e.g. 'a graphic designer creates static visual assets such as logos, layouts and typography for print or digital use, whereas an animator uses specialist software to create moving images or motion graphics'). A fully developed answer with an applied example scores 3 marks (e.g. add 'for instance, on a film poster campaign, the graphic designer would create the poster layout and typography, while an animator would produce the title sequence motion graphics for the trailer'). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens during the post-production phase of a film production. Give one example of a specific task carried out at this stage.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): post-production is the stage after filming is complete, where raw footage is assembled into the finished product through editing; it also includes audio mixing, sound design, adding visual effects and motion graphics, colour grading and quality review before final delivery (2 marks for a developed description covering multiple processes; 1 mark for a basic statement such as 'the footage is edited').
Example (up to 2 marks): for example, a colourist adjusts the colour and contrast of each shot in software such as DaVinci Resolve so all scenes look visually consistent, even if they were filmed on different days or in different lighting conditions (2 marks for a specific, developed example; 1 mark for a vague example). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A small media company has been asked to produce a 3-minute promotional video for a local charity. The team consists of a producer, a director, a videographer and an editor.

Discuss how each job role contributes to the successful completion of this project across the three phases of production.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A balanced discussion that links specific job roles to specific tasks within at least two of the three phases, applied to the charity video scenario. For example: the producer sets the schedule and manages the charity client relationship throughout all phases; the director shapes the visual approach in pre-production (concept, storyboard) and directs filming during production; the editor assembles and grades the footage in post-production. Contrast or complexity should be present, e.g. noting that on a small team these roles may overlap, creating scheduling tension.
Secure (3-4 marks): At least two roles described with tasks across phases, with some reference to the scenario.
Developing (2 marks): One role or one phase described with limited detail.
Emerging (1 mark): A vague statement about the team with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A media student argues that pre-production is the most important phase of the production workflow because it determines the success of everything that follows.

Evaluate the extent to which thorough pre-production planning leads to a higher-quality finished media product.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced evaluation that argues thorough pre-production is crucial because it identifies problems early, aligns the team around a shared creative vision, and ensures resources (locations, assets, budget) are secured before expensive production begins; then challenges this with the counter-argument that even outstanding planning cannot fully account for creative decisions made during production (a director may change approach when filming) or post-production discoveries (unexpected footage may produce a better edit). A substantiated judgement is reached about the relationship between planning and quality, going beyond a simple list.
Secure (5-6 marks): At least two well-developed points on each side with an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points on the value of pre-production with limited counter-argument.
Emerging (1-2 marks): A basic statement about planning with no development or evaluation. [8 marks]

before.exam_tip_html: When describing a job role, always state clearly what that person does, not just their job title. Examiners want to see understanding: writing "the editor assembles footage, applies colour grading and adds music to create the final cut" scores more than "the editor edits the video". For questions about the production workflow, name the phase and then give at least two specific tasks from that phase — this is especially important for "describe" and "explain" questions worth 3 or more marks.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a demographic variable used to profile a target audience?
A) Production budget
B) Age
C) File format
D) Post-production software
practice_questions.marks: B) Age [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two pieces of information that a client brief typically provides to a media producer.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct correct answers, for example: the purpose of the product (e.g. to promote, inform, entertain) [1]; the target audience [1]; content requirements [1]; the deadline [1]; the budget [1]; technical specifications such as file format or dimensions [1]; brand guidelines such as colours or fonts [1]. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why identifying the target audience is important when planning a media product.
practice_questions.marks: A basic point scores 1 mark (e.g. 'so the designer knows who the product is for'). Development scores 2 marks (e.g. 'knowing the target audience's age group allows the designer to choose an appropriate language register — informal and direct for teenagers, formal and professional for business clients'). A fully developed answer with an applied example scores 3 marks (e.g. add 'for a children's educational app aimed at ages 7-10, this means using simple vocabulary, large touch-friendly buttons and bright, primary colours, which would be inappropriate for a product targeting adult professionals'). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by 'audience segmentation'. Give one example of how a media company might use it.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): audience segmentation is the process of dividing a large audience into distinct sub-groups based on shared characteristics (e.g. age, interests, income) so that different messages or product versions can be tailored to each group (2 marks for a clear, developed description; 1 mark for a basic statement such as 'splitting the audience into groups').
Example (up to 2 marks): for example, a streaming platform segments its audience by age and recommends animated content and family films to users under 12, while recommending documentaries and crime dramas to adults aged 35-50, increasing engagement for each sub-group (2 marks for a specific, developed example; 1 mark for a vague example). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A local gym has provided a brief for a new promotional video. The brief states that the target audience is adults aged 18-35 who are interested in fitness and health, and who primarily use social media on their smartphones.

Discuss how this target audience information should influence the design and production decisions for the promotional video.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A balanced discussion covering at least two distinct design or production decisions, each clearly linked to a specific demographic detail from the brief. For example: the mobile-first audience means the video should be produced in a vertical (9:16) format for Instagram Reels or TikTok, with text large enough to read on a small screen; the 18-35 age group and fitness interest means dynamic, fast-paced editing with upbeat music rather than slow, corporate-style pacing. Contrast should be present, e.g. noting the tension between keeping the video short enough for social media attention spans (under 60 seconds) and including enough content to be persuasive.
Secure (3-4 marks): Two design decisions identified and linked to the audience profile with some development.
Developing (2 marks): One decision identified with limited audience linkage.
Emerging (1 mark): A vague reference to the target audience. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A media student claims that understanding the target audience is the single most important factor in determining the success of a media product.

Evaluate the extent to which you agree with this claim.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced evaluation that argues audience understanding is fundamental because it drives every creative decision (format, platform, language, tone, colour, content) and a product that fails to connect with its audience will not achieve its purpose regardless of technical quality; then challenges this with counter-arguments that other factors are equally or more critical in some contexts — such as meeting all client requirements (a product perfectly matched to its audience but late or over budget has failed), or that technical quality and originality can create audience demand (the audience does not always know what it wants until it sees it, as seen in groundbreaking media works). A clear, substantiated judgement is reached.
Secure (5-6 marks): Points on both sides with an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant but largely one-sided points.
Emerging (1-2 marks): A basic statement with no evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of a colour code used to communicate danger or urgency?
A) Blue
B) Green
C) Red
D) White
practice_questions.marks: C) Red [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two visual codes that a media creator can use to communicate meaning to an audience.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct correct code types, for example: colour [1]; typography / font choice [1]; layout [1]; imagery / photography style [1]; camera angle or shot size [1]. Answers must name a code type, not just describe a specific product. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by a 'genre convention' and why it matters to a media creator.
practice_questions.marks: A basic point scores 1 mark (e.g. 'a convention is something that is expected in a type of media'). Development scores 2 marks (e.g. 'a genre convention is an established characteristic that audiences recognise and expect from a particular type of media product, such as low-key lighting in horror films or bright colours in children's TV shows'). A fully developed answer with an applied reason scores 3 marks (e.g. add 'it matters to a creator because following conventions makes a product immediately legible to the right audience, who uses those codes to decide whether the product is for them; breaking conventions without intent risks alienating the audience'). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how a media creator can use typography to communicate the style and tone of a media product. Give one example to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): typography communicates through the choice of font style and weight — serif fonts convey tradition and authority; sans-serif fonts feel modern and clean; handwritten or display fonts suggest personality, informality or creativity; letter spacing and font weight also contribute to the product's visual tone (2 marks for a developed description covering at least two aspects; 1 mark for a basic statement).
Example (up to 2 marks): for example, a law firm's website uses a bold serif font such as Georgia to convey authority and trustworthiness, whereas a children's toy brand uses a rounded, playful sans-serif font to feel approachable and fun — two products using typography to communicate opposite tones (2 marks for a specific, contrasting example; 1 mark for a vague reference). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A media student is designing a poster for a new horror video game. The target audience is male gamers aged 16-24.

Discuss how media codes and genre conventions should influence the design decisions for this poster.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A balanced discussion that applies at least two distinct code types to the horror genre and the specific target audience, with justification for each. For example: colour codes (dark palette of black, red and grey to signify danger and tension, typical of horror genre conventions) alongside imagery codes (isolated figure, obscured face to build threat and mystery, matching audience expectations from the horror genre) and typography (jagged or distressed font to reinforce unease). Discussion should acknowledge the specific demographic (male gamers 16-24) and how it shapes choices beyond generic horror conventions.
Secure (3-4 marks): Two code types discussed with some genre and audience linkage.
Developing (2 marks): One code described with limited explanation.
Emerging (1 mark): A vague reference to horror without specific code analysis. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Some media theorists argue that genre conventions restrict creativity by forcing creators to produce predictable, formulaic products.

Evaluate the extent to which genre conventions limit or enable creativity in media production.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced evaluation that argues conventions restrict creativity by creating pressure to conform to expected formulas, reducing originality and making products feel repetitive; then challenges this by arguing conventions are a creative resource — knowing them thoroughly is what allows creators to subvert them for artistic effect (parody, genre-blending, deliberate subversion), and that working within a framework can drive creativity rather than suppress it. A clear, substantiated judgement is reached about whether the benefits of conventions outweigh the restrictions, with specific examples from real or realistic media products.
Secure (5-6 marks): Points on both sides with some example use and an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points largely one-sided, limited examples.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic statements with no development or evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which organisation provides age ratings for video games sold in the UK?
A) BBFC
B) Ofcom
C) PEGI
D) ASA
practice_questions.marks: C) PEGI [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two types of asset licence that allow a media creator to use material they did not create.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct correct answers, for example: royalty-free licence [1]; Creative Commons licence [1]; commercially licensed/permission-based licence [1]; public domain (no licence required) [1]. Answers must name a specific licence type; "stock images" alone scores zero without specifying the licence. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by a Creative Commons (CC) licence and give one example of how it restricts use.
practice_questions.marks: A basic point scores 1 mark (e.g. 'a Creative Commons licence lets you use someone else's work'). Development scores 2 marks (e.g. 'a Creative Commons licence is a standardised set of permissions granted by the copyright holder that allows others to use the work under defined conditions without seeking individual permission'). A fully developed answer with a specific restriction scores 3 marks (e.g. add 'for example, a CC BY-NC licence allows use of the work as long as the original creator is attributed and the work is not used for any commercial purpose — so a student could use it in a school project but a company could not use it in a paid advertisement'). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between a PEGI rating and a BBFC certificate. Give one example of a rating from each system.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): PEGI is the Pan European Game Information system and classifies video games; the BBFC (British Board of Film Classification) classifies films and video works for cinema and home release. Both systems use age-based categories, but PEGI applies specifically to games and the BBFC to films (2 marks for a clear distinction naming both bodies and their scope; 1 mark for identifying only one).
Examples (1 mark each): PEGI example — e.g. a PEGI 16 rating means the game is not suitable for players under 16 and is legally enforced at UK retail; BBFC example — e.g. a BBFC 15 certificate means only those aged 15 and over may see the film at a UK cinema, and this is legally enforced. [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A media student is producing a short documentary about life in their local town. They plan to film people in a shopping centre, use a popular song as background music and include photographs they found on an image-sharing website.

Discuss the legal and ethical considerations the student must address before publishing the documentary.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A balanced discussion covering at least two distinct legal or ethical issues, applied to the scenario. For example: copyright in the popular music track requires a licence — the student cannot simply use a chart song without permission or payment, and must source a royalty-free or Creative Commons alternative; the photographs from the image-sharing website require checking the licence attached to each image (CC licence terms or royalty-free status). Ethical dimension: filming identifiable people in the shopping centre without consent raises privacy concerns, and publishing their images could require model releases. Both issues should be developed with reasoning and scenario application.
Secure (3-4 marks): Two issues identified and briefly explained with some scenario reference.
Developing (2 marks): One issue identified with limited development.
Emerging (1 mark): A vague point about legal issues with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A games developer has created a first-person action game that features realistic violence and strong language. The developer believes age ratings are an unnecessary restriction on creative freedom and that players should decide for themselves what content is appropriate.

Evaluate the extent to which age ratings such as PEGI benefit both the games industry and its audiences.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced evaluation that argues age ratings benefit the industry by providing clear, trusted guidance to parents and consumers (reducing returns and complaints), protecting the industry from government censorship by demonstrating self-regulation, and enabling developers to create adult content for adult audiences without fear of the whole market being restricted; then challenges this by engaging with the developer's counter-argument that ratings can restrict creative expression, create commercial barriers for smaller studios who cannot afford classification fees, and that digital distribution (direct download, streaming) makes enforcement increasingly difficult. A clear, substantiated judgement is reached about the overall benefit of ratings systems, going beyond a simple list.
Secure (5-6 marks): Points on both sides with some application to the games industry and an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points largely one-sided; limited engagement with the counter-argument.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic statements about ratings with no development or evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which pre-production document is best suited to planning the layout of a poster?
A) Mind map
B) Storyboard
C) Visualisation diagram
D) Mood board
practice_questions.marks: C) Visualisation diagram [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two things that a mood board typically includes.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two of: images / photographs; colour swatches / colour palette; font samples / typography examples; texture references; brief annotations / notes explaining choices. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why completing pre-production planning documents is important before starting to create a media product.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks. Simple point (1 mark): e.g. 'it helps you stay on track'. Development (2 marks): e.g. 'pre-production documents such as a visualisation diagram show exactly what the finished product should look like, so the creator does not waste time making assets that do not fit the brief'. Further development or a second distinct reason with applied example (3 marks): e.g. add 'showing a mood board to a client before production starts means any disagreements about style are resolved early, avoiding costly re-working once the product has been partially built'. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what a visualisation diagram is and give one example of a product for which it would be used.
practice_questions.marks: Description (up to 2 marks): a rough sketch showing the planned layout of a static media product, including the position of images, text and colour areas, with annotations explaining design choices (2 marks for a clear, developed description covering layout and annotation; 1 mark for a basic statement). Example (up to 2 marks): for example, a visualisation diagram for a film poster showing a large central image placeholder, the film title in a bold font at the top, a tagline below the image and the billing block at the bottom, with colour notes in the margins (2 marks for a specific, applied example; 1 mark for a vague reference). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A student is creating a promotional campaign for a new youth sports club. Before starting, they have produced only a mind map.

Discuss whether the mind map alone is sufficient pre-production planning for this project, or whether additional documents should also be produced.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5-6 marks): A balanced discussion covering the value of a mind map (helps explore all possible ideas, ensures the brief is fully considered before committing to a direction) alongside its limitations (does not show what the product will look like, does not confirm the visual style with the client, does not demonstrate layout decisions). Argues convincingly that additional documents — a mood board to establish visual style and a visualisation diagram to plan the specific layout — are also needed for a complete pre-production package. Both sides developed with reasoning and applied to the scenario. Secure (3-4 marks): At least two relevant points identified and briefly explained, with some reference to the scenario. Developing (2 marks): One or two points identified but not clearly explained. Emerging (1 mark): A single point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A media student has been given a brief to design a promotional poster for a school play. They are unsure whether to create a mood board or a visualisation diagram first.

Evaluate the relative importance of each pre-production document for this project, and justify which one the student should produce first.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7-8 marks): A sustained evaluation that clearly explains the purpose of each document (mood board = visual inspiration and style direction; visualisation diagram = specific layout of the poster), applies them to the school play brief, and makes a supported judgement about order. The strongest answers argue that the mood board should come first because agreeing the visual tone (colour palette, style) before committing to a layout avoids having to redraw the visualisation diagram if the style direction changes. Counter-argument acknowledged: a creator confident in the style might go straight to a visualisation diagram. The judgement is substantiated and goes beyond listing. Secure (5-6 marks): Both documents explained with some application to the scenario and an attempt at a reasoned judgement. Developing (3-4 marks): Both documents described but largely surface-level; limited application. Emerging (1-2 marks): One or both documents mentioned with minimal explanation and no evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which pre-production document is most appropriate for planning an animated short film?
A) Visualisation diagram
B) Mood board
C) Storyboard
D) Mind map
practice_questions.marks: C) Storyboard [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two pieces of information that should be included in a storyboard frame annotation.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two of: shot type; camera angle; duration / timing of the shot; camera movement (pan, tilt, zoom); transition to the next shot (cut, dissolve, fade); audio notes (dialogue, voiceover, music, sound effects). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a work plan should include contingency time.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks. Simple point (1 mark): e.g. 'in case something goes wrong'. Development (2 marks): e.g. 'contingency is buffer time built into the schedule to allow for unexpected problems such as equipment failure or the need to reshoot a scene'. Further development (3 marks): e.g. add 'without contingency, any single delay will cause all subsequent tasks to slip, making it impossible to meet the final client deadline, which could damage the creator's professional reputation'. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what a script includes for an audio-visual production, and give one example of how it helps during the production process.
practice_questions.marks: Description (up to 2 marks): a script sets out the spoken dialogue or voiceover word for word, alongside sound effect cues, music instructions and visual descriptions, formatted so performers and crew can follow it (2 marks for a clear, developed description; 1 mark for a basic statement). Example (up to 2 marks): for example, a client reviewing the script before filming begins can check that the product's message and tone match the brief, meaning any changes can be made on paper rather than after footage has been recorded (2 marks for a specific, applied example; 1 mark for a vague reference). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A student is producing a 90-second promotional video for a local business. The student has written a script but has not yet produced a storyboard or work plan.

Discuss whether the script alone is sufficient planning for this project.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5-6 marks): A balanced discussion identifying what the script provides (accurate dialogue, correct length, client-approved message before filming) alongside what it lacks (no visual plan for each shot, so the student does not know what shots to film or in what order; no time management, so there is no way to ensure the product is ready by the deadline). Argues convincingly that a storyboard is also needed to plan the visual sequence and a work plan to manage the production timeline. Both sides developed with reasoning applied to the 90-second video scenario. Secure (3-4 marks): At least two relevant points identified and briefly explained with some scenario reference. Developing (2 marks): One or two points but without clear explanation. Emerging (1 mark): A single basic point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A media production company has been commissioned to create a two-minute animated advertisement. The lead animator wants to skip the storyboarding stage to save time.

Evaluate the extent to which storyboarding is essential to the successful completion of this project.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7-8 marks): A sustained evaluation arguing that storyboarding is highly valuable for animation specifically because: every frame must be drawn from scratch (unlike live action, there is no camera improvisation), so errors discovered mid-animation are very costly to fix; the storyboard allows the client to approve the visual narrative before a single frame is animated; and it coordinates the team so that each animator works on the correct scenes in the correct order. Counter-argument: an experienced solo animator working on a simple product might argue that a rough sketch suffices and a full storyboard is time-consuming. However, for a commissioned, client-facing advertisement, the risks of skipping storyboarding outweigh the time saved. A clear, substantiated judgement is reached. Secure (5-6 marks): Both sides explained with application to animation and some judgement. Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points but largely one-sided or surface-level. Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points with no evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which image file format supports transparency and is most suitable for a logo to be placed on a coloured background?
A) JPEG
B) GIF
C) TIFF
D) PNG
practice_questions.marks: D) PNG [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two types of asset that a media creator might need to identify during the pre-production planning stage.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two of: images / photographs; audio clips / sound effects / music; video clips / footage; graphics / illustrations / diagrams; text / copy / headings. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why using sensible file naming conventions is important in a media production project.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks. Simple point (1 mark): e.g. 'so you can find files easily'. Development (2 marks): e.g. 'descriptive file names allow any member of the team to identify the correct version of an asset at a glance without opening every file in a folder'. Further development (3 marks): e.g. add 'version numbers in file names also prevent the accidental overwriting of a working file with a broken revision, which could mean hours of lost work with no way to recover the earlier version'. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between lossy and lossless compression. Give one example of a file format that uses each type.
practice_questions.marks: Description (up to 2 marks): lossy compression permanently removes some data to reduce file size, which means some quality is lost (the original cannot be perfectly reconstructed); lossless compression reduces file size without losing any data, so the original can be perfectly reconstructed (2 marks for a clear description of both; 1 mark for describing only one). Example (up to 2 marks): JPEG is a lossy format, used for web photographs where a small file size matters more than perfect quality; PNG is a lossless format, used for logos and graphics where sharp edges and transparency must be preserved exactly (2 marks for one correct example of each; 1 mark for one example only or one example with a vague description). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A student is creating a media product that includes a high-resolution photograph for print, a background music track for a web video, and a logo with a transparent background for use on a website.

Discuss which file format the student should use for each asset and why.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5-6 marks): A balanced discussion addressing all three assets: TIFF or high-quality JPEG for the print photograph (lossless or minimal compression needed for print quality); MP3 for the background music web track (lossy compression produces a small file suitable for streaming; WAV would be unnecessarily large); PNG for the logo (lossless, supports transparency, sharp edges preserved). Each choice is justified with a relevant property (compression type, file size, transparency, quality). Answers that acknowledge trade-offs (e.g. JPEG could work for print at maximum quality setting, but TIFF is safer) score higher. Secure (3-4 marks): At least two assets addressed with correct format and brief justification. Developing (2 marks): One asset addressed correctly or formats stated without justification. Emerging (1 mark): A single point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A media student working on a team project has been using their own file naming system, which includes spaces and informal names such as 'background music final.mp3' and 'poster image v2 use this.jpg'.

Evaluate the impact of poor file management on a team media project and justify what a good file management system should include.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7-8 marks): A sustained evaluation identifying specific problems caused by poor naming (spaces in filenames break web links and script references; informal names like 'use this' cannot be read by a team member who does not know the context; no consistent version numbering means earlier working versions are lost if overwritten). Argues convincingly for a good system including: descriptive names without spaces (use hyphens or underscores); version numbers appended to each file; agreed naming convention documented at project start; logical sub-folder structure separating images, audio, exports etc. Counter-argument: for a solo project, less rigorous naming may cause fewer immediate problems. However, for team work and client handover, the investment in file management is always justified. Clear judgement reached with specific reference to the student scenario. Secure (5-6 marks): Both problems and solutions explained with scenario application and some judgement. Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points but largely one-sided. Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points with minimal development. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
What is the minimum recommended resolution for an image that will be printed in a professional publication?
A) 72 DPI
B) 150 DPI
C) 300 DPI
D) 600 PPI
practice_questions.marks: C) 300 DPI [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two technical properties of a digital image that affect its file size.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two of: resolution (DPI/PPI); dimensions (pixel width and height); bit depth / colour depth; compression type (lossy or lossless); file format. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by lossy compression and give one disadvantage of using it.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks. Simple point (1 mark): e.g. 'lossy compression removes some data'. Development (2 marks): e.g. 'lossy compression permanently removes data that is judged least noticeable, reducing file size at the cost of some quality that cannot be recovered'. Disadvantage with further development (3 marks): e.g. 'one disadvantage is generation loss: each time a JPEG is re-saved, another round of compression is applied, and the cumulative quality loss produces visible artefacts such as blockiness around edges after several edits'. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what bit depth means in the context of a digital image, and give one example of how different bit depths are used in practice.
practice_questions.marks: Description (up to 2 marks): bit depth is the number of bits used to represent the colour of each pixel; a higher bit depth means more possible colours and therefore more accurate colour representation, but a larger file size (2 marks for a developed description covering number of colours and the quality/size trade-off; 1 mark for a basic statement). Example (up to 2 marks): an 8-bit image can display 256 colours and is suitable for a simple logo or GIF animation; a 24-bit image (true colour) can display over 16 million colours and is used for photographs where subtle colour gradations must be preserved accurately (2 marks for a specific, applied example; 1 mark for one example only or a vague description). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A student has created a 10-minute video for a school website. The exported file is 4 GB and takes over three minutes to load. The student needs to reduce the file size while keeping the quality acceptable for web streaming.

Discuss the technical changes the student could make to reduce the file size without significantly affecting the viewer's experience.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5-6 marks): A balanced discussion covering at least two relevant technical changes with justification: reducing the bitrate (e.g. from a broadcast-quality 50 Mbps to a web-appropriate 5-8 Mbps for 1080p) eliminates most of the file size; reducing the output resolution from 4K to 1080p would also significantly reduce size with no visible difference on a standard school monitor; using H.264 encoding in an MP4 container applies efficient lossy compression appropriate for web delivery. Acknowledges the trade-off: too low a bitrate produces visible artefacts and buffering. Applied to the school-website scenario. Secure (3-4 marks): At least two changes identified and briefly justified. Developing (2 marks): One change identified, limited justification. Emerging (1 mark): A single point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A graphic designer is preparing a set of images for both a printed brochure and a company website. The same photograph will appear in both publications.

Evaluate the decisions the designer should make about resolution, file format and compression for each version of the image, and justify why the two versions must be prepared differently.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7-8 marks): A sustained evaluation covering all three properties for each output. Print version: 300 DPI; TIFF or high-quality JPEG (minimal or no compression); larger file size is acceptable because the file is sent directly to the printer, not downloaded by a viewer. Web version: 72-96 PPI; JPEG with moderate lossy compression; dimensions reduced to the exact display size (e.g. 1200 x 800 px); small file size is essential so the page loads quickly. Justification for the difference: the viewer's experience differs — a print reader holds the image at close range and notices low resolution, whereas a web viewer on a standard monitor cannot distinguish a 72 PPI image from a 300 PPI image but will notice slow loading times. A clear judgement is reached that the different purposes require genuinely different technical specifications, not simply ‘one is better than the other’. Secure (5-6 marks): Both versions addressed with correct properties and some justification. Developing (3-4 marks): Surface-level description of one or both versions. Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points with no evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which distribution platform requires the audience to have an internet connection and automatically adjusts video quality to match connection speed?
A) Physical media (DVD)
B) Broadcast television
C) Streaming platforms using adaptive streaming
D) Print publication
practice_questions.marks: C) Streaming platforms using adaptive streaming [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two accessibility features that should be considered when distributing a video online.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two of: subtitles / closed captions; audio description / narration for visually impaired viewers; transcript provided alongside the video; high colour contrast for any on-screen text; compatible with screen readers. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of distributing a media product on a social media platform.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks. Advantage (1 mark with development = 2 marks): e.g. 'social media platforms allow content to be shared by followers to their own networks, dramatically extending reach beyond the creator's own audience at no additional cost'. Disadvantage (1 mark): e.g. 'social media platforms apply their own compression on upload, reducing image and video quality so the creator must export assets at very specific dimensions and quality settings for each platform'. A single well-developed point on one side scores 2 marks; a brief point on each side scores 2 marks; 3 marks requires a developed point on at least one side. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two factors that should be considered when choosing a distribution platform for a media product. Give one example for each factor.
practice_questions.marks: One mark per factor + one mark per example (up to 4 marks total). Acceptable factors and examples: Target audience / who can access the platform — e.g. if the audience is elderly people with limited internet access, physical media such as a printed brochure may be more appropriate than a social media post. File format compatibility — e.g. YouTube requires MP4 video files; uploading in an unsupported format means the video cannot be published. Cost — e.g. printing and posting physical DVDs incurs manufacturing and postage costs, whereas uploading to YouTube is free. Accessibility — e.g. a video platform that supports closed captions is more inclusive for d/Deaf viewers than one that does not. [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A student has created a 3-minute promotional video for a local charity. The charity wants to reach as wide an audience as possible, including older adults who may not use social media.

Discuss which distribution platforms would be most appropriate for the charity's promotional video.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5-6 marks): A balanced discussion identifying at least two platforms and evaluating each in relation to the scenario. YouTube or a website: large reach, free, accessible on smart TVs as well as computers and phones, accepted format is MP4, supports captions — suitable for the general public including older adults who do use the internet. Social media (Facebook specifically): older adults are actually one of the largest Facebook demographics, so this may reach more of the target group than TikTok would; shares can extend reach virally. Physical media (DVD or printed flyer): appropriate for older adults without internet access, but expensive to produce and cannot be easily updated. Acknowledges the trade-off between digital (wide reach, low cost) and physical (accessible without internet, higher cost). Applied to the charity scenario. Secure (3-4 marks): Two platforms identified with brief justification and some scenario link. Developing (2 marks): One platform or general points without scenario application. Emerging (1 mark): A single point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A games developer has created an interactive educational quiz for secondary school students. They are deciding whether to distribute the quiz via a website, a dedicated app on the Apple App Store, or on physical USB drives sent to schools.

Evaluate the suitability of each distribution method for this product and audience, and recommend which option the developer should choose.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7-8 marks): A sustained evaluation of all three options. Website: low cost, instant updates possible, no download required, works on any device with a browser — but relies on school internet connectivity, which may be unreliable; no revenue model without a subscription. App store: large built-in audience, trusted payment system, works offline once downloaded — but requires a developer fee, review process, and two separate builds for iOS and Android; schools may restrict app installation on managed devices. USB drives: works without internet, can be used on any computer — but expensive to produce, cannot be updated once distributed, risk of data being copied or the drive being lost; no analytics on usage. A clear, substantiated recommendation is reached (website is likely the strongest choice for a school audience given device variety and the ability to update content), with counter-arguments acknowledged. Secure (5-6 marks): All three options addressed with some application and an attempt at a recommendation. Developing (3-4 marks): Two options addressed, limited application. Emerging (1-2 marks): One option or basic points with no evaluation. [8 marks]
